query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: In multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, a transient chemical short-range order develops under high-temperature catalytic or thermoelectric conditions (473–1923 K) in reactive or inert atmospheres. This short-range order reduces interdiffusion and phase-separation kinetics, thereby governing their structural and chemical stability during extended thermal cycling in catalytic and thermoelectric service regimes.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-element near-equiatomic nanoparticles (e.g., 3–5 principal metallic components) with a single-phase solid-solution structure and minimal initial compositional segregation, as prepared by standard colloidal or chemical synthesis routes.
generation.intervention: Subject these nanoparticles to repeated temperature cycling (e.g., 300–1923 K) under controlled chemical-potential gradients (reducing or oxidizing atmospheres) while performing in-situ electron microscopy or X-ray diffraction and complementary DFT-based simulations.
generation.conditions: Thermal cycles from 473 K to 1923 K in alternating inert (Ar) and reactive (e.g., H2-rich or O2-rich) environments over tens of cycles, each held for extended dwell times to mimic catalytic or thermoelectric operational conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Transient chemical short-range ordering and the kinetic barriers it imposes on long-range diffusive processes like phase separation, grain coarsening, or surface segregation.
generation.mechanism: Local compositional rearrangements reduce atomic mobility through high mixing entropy and partial short-range ordering of dissimilar atoms, stabilizing the single-phase structure and limiting interfacial or surface-driven transformations.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to baseline monometallic or conventional binary/ternary reference nanoparticles, the multi-element near-equiatomic nanoparticles will exhibit delayed or suppressed phase separation, smaller grain growth, and compositional uniformity retention after multiple thermal cycles.
generation.baseline: Monometallic or simpler multi-component nanoparticles (e.g., standard Pt/Al2O3 catalysts or Ni–Cr alloys in thermoelectric devices) that typically show earlier phase transformations or higher extent of grain coarsening under comparable conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesized short-range-order-driven stabilization mechanism is expected to hold for nominally single-phase near-equiatomic nanoparticles with minimal initial segregation, at sizes under ~20 nm, and for operational temperatures up to about 1900 K. Beyond this range, entropic contributions or local ordering may no longer adequately suppress diffusion-limited coarsening or phase separation.
generation.uncertainty: Although indirect observations of persistent solid-solution phases exist in related multi-component alloys, it remains unclear if the same entropic effects suppress transformations in nanoparticle systems over numerous cycles without coarsening, warranting direct in-situ tests to confirm or refute the proposed mechanism.

falsification_experiment.design: Use in-situ high-temperature TEM or X-ray diffraction to track subgrain evolution and compositional changes across multiple thermal cycles between 473–1923 K, under mixing hydrogen/oxygen or inert gases to induce variable chemical-potential gradients. Compare near-equiatomic nanoparticles to conventional alloys and track structural changes, lattice parameters, and elemental partitioning in situ.
measurements: 1. Time-resolved diffraction patterns during each temperature dwell to detect phase transformations or lattice parameter changes.
2. Atomic resolution in-situ TEM or APT measurements of local elemental distributions to detect short-range ordering or segregation.
3. Particle size distributions before and after repeated cycling to quantify coarsening.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the near-equiatomic nanoparticles exhibit significant phase decomposition, pronounced particle growth, or loss of homogeneity at temperatures at or below ~1923 K and under tested chemical-potential gradients, contrary to the reference alloys’ behavior, the proposed short-range-order-based stabilization mechanism would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In the quest of new materials that can withstand severe irradiation and mechanical extremes for advanced applications ( e.g . fission & fusion reactors, space applications, etc.), design, prediction and control of advanced materials beyond current material designs become paramount. Here, through a combined experimental and simulation methodology, we design a nanocrystalline refractory high entropy alloy (RHEA) system. Compositions assessed under extreme environments and in situ electron-microscopy reveal both high thermal stability and radiation resistance. We observe grain refinement under heavy ion irradiation and resistance to dual-beam irradiation and helium implantation in the form of low defect generation and evolution, as well as no detectable grain growth. The experimental and modeling results—showing a good agreement—can be applied to design and rapidly assess other alloys subjected to extreme environmental conditions. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Power stations

Polymorphism, which describes the occurrence of different lattice structures in a crystalline material, is a critical phenomenon in materials science and condensed matter physics. Recently, configuration disorder was compositionally engineered into single lattices, leading to the discovery of high-entropy alloys and high-entropy oxides. For these novel entropy-stabilized forms of crystalline matter with extremely high structural stability, is polymorphism still possible? Here by employing in situ high-pressure synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction, we reveal a polymorphic transition from face-centred-cubic ( fcc ) structure to hexagonal-close-packing ( hcp ) structure in the prototype CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy. The transition is irreversible, and our in situ high-temperature synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction experiments at different pressures of the retained hcp high-entropy alloy reveal that the fcc phase is a stable polymorph at high temperatures, while the hcp structure is more thermodynamically favourable at lower temperatures. As pressure is increased, the critical temperature for the hcp -to- fcc transformation also rises.

Unlike other conventional alloys based on a “principal element,” high-entropy alloy (HEA) is a unique material that maintains a random solid solution structure without forming intermetallic compounds in operating temperatures due to its high configurational entropy [1] – [3] . It also has outstanding physical and chemical properties, which makes it a potential replacement for traditional metallic materials, and it has recently been referred to as a multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) or compositionally concentrated alloy (CCA) [4] – [9] .

As attention in HEAs increases, many studies have been conducted to explore its mechanical, physical and chemical properties [10] – [15] . In particular, equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, which was the first developed HEA, is the most studied because of its excellent combination of tensile strength and elongation along with excellent fracture toughness and corrosion resistance [6] , [16] – [21] . However, despite the advantages of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, many issues arise owing to its low yield strength and costly and complex thermomechanical processing (i.e., multiple casting → hot rolling → homogenization → cold rolling → annealing → cutting, etc.

Metallic alloys containing multiple principal alloying elements, which are known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [1] – [3] , have attracted extensive research interest in recent years with many studies focused on their microstructure, mechanical properties, and underlying deformation mechanisms [4] – [6] . For example, as a new class of structural materials, certain face-centered cubic ( fcc ) alloys, in particular CrCoNi-based HEAs, have been shown to possess improved strength and exceptional damage tolerance, especially at cryogenic temperatures [7] , [8] .

A second prominent class of HEA systems are refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), which comprise mostly refractory elements and invariably crystallize as body-centered cubic ( bcc ) solid solutions; these alloys have been considered as promising candidate materials for elevated-temperature applications due to their exceptional resistance to softening and extremely high melting points [9] – [11] .
